The factors, so you can do it yourself next time: a mile is 1.609 km, so a marathon's 26.2 miles is 42.2 km and 10 km is 6.2 miles. Celsius to Fahrenheit is × 1.8 + 32, so 20 °C is 68 °F, and the other way is (F − 32) ÷ 1.8, so 100 °F is 37.8 °C. For four people: 200 g plain flour, 2 tablespoons sugar, 2 teaspoons baking powder and half a teaspoon of salt in one bowl; 300 ml milk, one egg and 30 g melted butter in another. Combine them with a few strokes and stop while it is still lumpy - overmixing is what makes pancakes tough. Rest the batter five minutes while a pan heats over medium. Ladle about 60 ml each, flip when the bubbles on top pop and stay open, and give the second side a minute. Butter and syrup, and blueberries dropped on after ladling rather than stirred in.

The ones people reach for: a passable email check is ^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+$; a US phone number is ^\(?\d{3}\)?[-. ]?\d{3}[-. ]?\d{4}$; an ISO date is ^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$; an issue key like OPS-7 is \b[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+\b. The pieces: ^ and $ anchor the ends, \d is a digit, \w a word character, + means one or more, ? optional, and (?: ) groups without capturing. If you give me three strings that should match and three that should not, I will write the exact pattern and test it against them.

The trade is real, and it helps to name it. Remote gives back the commute, protects deep work, widens hiring and lets people with caring responsibilities keep their jobs. The office gives fast informal alignment, ambient context, and mentoring that new people mostly get by overhearing. Remote teams that work well replace what the office gave for free: decisions written down, a few fixed overlap hours, casual conversation scheduled on purpose, and a real offsite a couple of times a year. Hybrid without a rule about which days tends to be the worst of both.

The things with the best evidence are unglamorous. Keep the same wake time every day, including weekends; it anchors everything else. Get daylight within an hour of waking. Stop caffeine by early afternoon - its half-life is about five hours. Keep the room cool and dark. If you are awake more than twenty minutes, get up and do something dull in low light rather than lie there teaching your brain that bed is for worrying. If it has lasted more than a few weeks, talk to a doctor; CBT for insomnia has better results than any medication.

By family: 2xx means it worked (200 OK, 201 created, 204 nothing to return). 3xx means go elsewhere (301 permanently, 302 for now, 304 your cached copy is still good). 4xx means the request is the problem (400 malformed, 401 not signed in, 403 signed in but not allowed, 404 not here, 405 wrong method, 409 conflict, 429 slow down). 5xx means the server is the problem (500 it crashed, 502 the proxy could not reach it, 503 overloaded or in maintenance, 504 it timed out). So: 4xx, fix what you sent; 5xx, retry or page someone.

DNS turns a name into an address. Your machine asks a resolver; the resolver asks the root, then the top-level domain, then the authoritative server for that zone, caching each answer for its time-to-live. The record types you will meet: A and AAAA for addresses, CNAME for an alias, MX for mail, TXT for verification strings, NS for who is authoritative. Most "the site is down" reports that are not really down are DNS - a stale cache, a mistyped CNAME, or a TTL nobody lowered before a migration.

With customers and orders:

SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;

INNER keeps only customers who have orders. LEFT JOIN keeps every customer and fills the order columns with NULL where there is none, which is how you find customers who have never bought: add WHERE o.id IS NULL. FULL OUTER keeps the unmatched rows from both sides. One subtlety worth knowing: a filter on the right-hand table belongs in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN, or it quietly turns back into an INNER JOIN.

It depends on what you want to keep. To drop the commit but keep the changes staged: git reset --soft HEAD~1. To keep them unstaged: git reset HEAD~1. To discard the changes too: git reset --hard HEAD~1, and be certain first. If the commit has already been pushed to a branch others use, do not rewrite it - git revert HEAD makes a new commit that undoes it. To fix only the message or add a forgotten file, git commit --amend. And whatever you reset stays in git reflog for weeks, so very little is truly lost.

The commands that cover most days: kubectl get pods -n <namespace> to see what is running (add -o wide for nodes); kubectl describe pod <name> for the events, which is where the real error usually is; kubectl logs <pod> -f, and --previous for the container that just crashed; kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh for a shell; kubectl apply -f for declaring what you want; kubectl rollout status and rollout undo for deployments; kubectl port-forward to reach a service locally. Set a default namespace once with kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=<ns> and stop typing -n.
